You label each sentence of one passage from a novel. Judge each sentence by what it says and how it is said here. Do not use outside knowledge of the novel.

For every numbered sentence give two labels: its feeling, then its pace.

feeling:
- warm: the sentence shows affection, kindness, pleasure, praise or ease between people.
- cold: the sentence shows dislike, contempt, anger, hurt, mockery or distance between people.
- neither: it shows neither, or you cannot tell.

pace:
- tense: something is at stake or unsettled in the sentence: a conflict, a worry, suspense, or strong feeling held back.
- calm: nothing is at stake in the sentence.

Label every sentence, including short ones.

PASSAGE:
<<<
[1] It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.

[2] However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

[3] “My dear Mr. Ashby,” said his lady to him one day, “have you heard that Brierley Park is let at last?”

[4] Mr. Ashby replied that he had not.

[5] “But it is,” returned she; “for Mrs. Penrose has just been here, and she told me all about it.”

[6] Mr. Ashby made no answer.

[7] “Do not you want to know who has taken it?” cried his wife, impatiently.

[8] “_You_ want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it.”

[9] This was invitation enough.

[10] “Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Penrose says that Brierley is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it that he agreed with Mr. Lindsey immediately; that he is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week.”

[11] “What is his name?”

[12] “Calder.”

[13] “Is he married or single?”

[14] “Oh, single, my dear, to be sure! [15] A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year. [16] What a fine thing for our girls!”

[17] “How so? how can it affect them?”

[18] “My dear Mr. Ashby,” replied his wife, “how can you be so tiresome? [19] You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”

[20] “Is that his design in settling here?”

[21] “Design? [22] Nonsense, how can you talk so! [23] But it is very likely that he _may_ fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as soon as he comes.”

[24] “I see no occasion for that. [25] You and the girls may go--or you may send them by themselves, which perhaps will be still better; for as you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Calder might like you the best of the party.”
>>>

Label sentences 1 to 25.

[1] “My dear, you flatter me. [2] I certainly _have_ had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now. [3] When a woman has five grown-up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty.”

[4] “In such cases, a woman has not often much beauty to think of.”

[5] “But, my dear, you must indeed go and see Mr. Calder when he comes into the neighbourhood.”

[6] “It is more than I engage for, I assure you.”

[7] “But consider your daughters. [8] Only think what an establishment it would be for one of them. [9] Sir Cyril and Lady Jessop are determined to go, merely on that account; for in general, you know, they visit no new comers. [10] Indeed you must go, for it will be impossible for _us_ to visit him, if you do not.”

[11] “You are over scrupulous, surely. [12] I dare say Mr. Calder will be very glad to see you; and I will send a few lines by you to assure him of my hearty consent to his marrying whichever he chooses of the girls--though I must throw in a good word for my little Clara.”

[13] “I desire you will do no such thing. [14] Clara is not a bit better than the others: and I am sure she is not half so handsome as Edith, nor half so good-humoured as Flora. [15] But you are always giving _her_ the preference.”

[16] “They have none of them much to recommend them,” replied he: “they are all silly and ignorant like other girls; but Clara has something more of quickness than her sisters.”

[17] “Mr. Ashby, how can you abuse your own children in such a way? [18] You take delight in vexing me. [19] You have no compassion on my poor nerves.”

[20] “You mistake me, my dear. [21] I have a high respect for your nerves. [22] They are my old friends. [23] I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least.”

[24] “Ah, you do not know what I suffer.”

[25] “But I hope you will get over it, and live to see many young men of four thousand a year come into the neighbourhood.”

[26] “It will be no use to us, if twenty such should come, since you will not visit them.”

[27] “Depend upon it, my dear, that when there are twenty, I will visit them all.”

[28] Mr. Ashby was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three-and-twenty years had been insufficient to make his wife understand his character. [29] _Her_ mind was less difficult to develope. [30] She was a woman of mean understanding, little information, and uncertain temper. [31] When she was discontented, she fancied herself nervous. [32] The business of her life was to get her daughters married: its solace was visiting and news.
>>>

[2] He had always intended to visit him, though to the last always assuring his wife that he should not go; and till the evening after the visit was paid she had no knowledge of it. [3] It was then disclosed in the following manner. [4] Observing his second daughter employed in trimming a hat, he suddenly addressed her with,--

[5] “I hope Mr. Calder will like it, Clara.”

[6] “We are not in a way to know _what_ Mr. Calder likes,” said her mother, resentfully, “since we are not to visit.”

[7] “But you forget, mamma,” said Agnes, “that we shall meet him at the assemblies, and that Mrs. Penrose has promised to introduce him.”

[8] “I do not believe Mrs. Penrose will do any such thing. [9] She has two nieces of her own. [10] She is a selfish, hypocritical woman, and I have no opinion of her.”

[11] “No more have I,” said Mr. Ashby; “and I am glad to find that you do not depend on her serving you.”

[12] Mrs. Ashby deigned not to make any reply; but, unable to contain herself, began scolding one of her daughters.

[13] “Don’t keep coughing so, Garside, for heaven’s sake! [14] Have a little compassion on my nerves. [15] You tear them to pieces.”

[16] “Garside has no discretion in her coughs,” said her father; “she times them ill.”

[17] “I do not cough for my own amusement,” replied Garside, fretfully. [18] “When is your next ball to be, Clara?”

[19] “To-morrow fortnight.”

[20] “Ay, so it is,” cried her mother, “and Mrs. Penrose does not come back till the day before; so, it will be impossible for her to introduce him, for she will not know him herself.”

[21] “Then, my dear, you may have the advantage of your friend, and introduce Mr. Calder to _her_.”

[22] “Impossible, Mr. Ashby, impossible, when I am not acquainted with him myself; how can you be so teasing?”

[23] “I honour your circumspection. [24] A fortnight’s acquaintance is certainly very little. [25] One cannot know what a man really is by the end of a fortnight. [26] But if _we_ do not venture, somebody else will; and after all, Mrs. Penrose and her nieces must stand their chance; and, therefore, as she will think it an act of kindness, if you decline the office, I will take it on myself.”

[3] “What can be the meaning of that emphatic exclamation?” cried he. [4] “Do you consider the forms of introduction, and the stress that is laid on them, as nonsense? [5] I cannot quite agree with you _there_. [6] What say you, Kirby? [7] For you are a young lady of deep reflection, I know, and read great books, and make extracts.”

[8] Kirby wished to say something very sensible, but knew not how.

[9] “While Kirby is adjusting her ideas,” he continued, “let us return to Mr. Calder.”

[10] “I am sick of Mr. Calder,” cried his wife.

[11] “I am sorry to hear _that_; but why did you not tell me so before? [12] If I had known as much this morning, I certainly would not have called on him. [13] It is very unlucky; but as I have actually paid the visit, we cannot escape the acquaintance now.”

[14] The astonishment of the ladies was just what he wished--that of Mrs. Ashby perhaps surpassing the rest; though when the first tumult of joy was over, she began to declare that it was what she had expected all the while.

[15] “How good it was in you, my dear Mr. Ashby! [16] But I knew I should persuade you at last. [17] I was sure you loved your girls too well to neglect such an acquaintance. [18] Well, how pleased I am! [19] And it is such a good joke, too, that you should have gone this morning, and never said a word about it till now.”

[20] “Now, Garside, you may cough as much as you choose,” said Mr. Ashby; and, as he spoke, he left the room, fatigued with the raptures of his wife.

[21] “What an excellent father you have, girls,” said she, when the door was shut. [22] “I do not know how you will ever make him amends for his kindness; or me either, for that matter. [23] At our time of life, it is not so pleasant, I can tell you, to be making new acquaintances every day; but for your sakes we would do anything. [24] Flora, my love, though you _are_ the youngest, I dare say Mr. Calder will dance with you at the next ball.”

[25] “Oh,” said Flora, stoutly, “I am not afraid; for though I _am_ the youngest, I’m the tallest.”

[26] The rest of the evening was spent in conjecturing how soon he would return Mr. Ashby’s visit, and determining when they should ask him to dinner.

[4] Ingram assured her friend of her satisfaction in being useful, and that it amply repaid her for the little sacrifice of her time. [5] This was very amiable; but Ingram’s kindness extended farther than Agnes had any conception of:--its object was nothing less than to secure her from any return of Mr. Ellery’s addresses, by engaging them towards herself. [6] Such was Miss Jessop’s scheme; and appearances were so favourable, that when they parted at night, she would have felt almost sure of success if he had not been to leave Hertfordshire so very soon. [11] But little had she dared to hope that so much love and eloquence awaited her there.

[13] The stupidity with which he was favoured by nature must guard his courtship from any charm that could make a woman wish for its continuance; and Miss Jessop, who accepted him solely from the pure and disinterested desire of an establishment, cared not how soon that establishment were gained.
